job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Uma Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My days are organised, because otherwise I'd go under. I have a spreadsheet of every application with the date, the contact, the follow-up and the result, and I check it each morning in the room I rent in a shared house in Calderbrook. I do two applications a day, then an hour of practice for the online tests, then a long walk. I did finance at Rowan University and I'm top of my year, with an internship in the operations team of a payments company and one at a tax practice. After five months I've sent 82 applications, had four interviews and no offer, and I owe 40,000.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that makes sense, since most new things get oversold. At home I'd say that jobs and prices would carry on the way they are. I'd leave it at that, because it doesn't change my week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd still be anxious, but for ordinary reasons. The spreadsheet says that graduate openings in my area are down maybe a third since last year, and the firms that do hire want a year of experience first. A plateau means the market stays like that, and that's not good for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd widen my search to include the civil service and the council finance teams, which hire on a fixed cycle and don't depend on a boss's mood. I'd also apply to places two or three hours away and consider moving if I got an offer. And I'd keep practising the online tests, since I've passed the first stage of four employers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty drained. I try to keep my feelings out of it, but the weeks without a reply start to weigh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep a spreadsheet of everything. What does it show about where the jobs are?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The spreadsheet shows that the big employers hire in September and January, and the rest of the year is mostly closed. Smaller firms reply less but are more likely to say yes, so I've shifted my time that way. The public sector hires slowly but fairly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are your parents' circumstances, if you don't mind my asking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad drives a taxi and my mum looks after my gran, so they have a tight budget and no spare cash. They'd help if they could, but they can't, and I'd feel awful asking. They're proud of the degree, which makes it harder.

say: New things get **oversold**, and a plateau doesn't change my week.
Jobs and prices would carry on the way they **are**.
think: Graduate openings near me are down about a **third**, and a plateau keeps it there.
Firms that hire want a year of **experience** first.
do: Widen the search to the **civil service** and council finance teams.
Apply to places two or three hours away and **move** for an offer.
feel: **Drained**: I keep feelings out of it, but the quiet weeks weigh.

fieldNote: Her **spreadsheet** gives real numbers, not just mood, and she acts on them.
Pragmatic: she moves to public sector and small firms based on **reply rates**.
Parents' tight budget means she will **not** ask for money.

steps.text: Apply to civil service and council finance teams this month
Apply to small firms two or three hours away
Practise the online tests every afternoon
Keep logging every application and follow-up in the spreadsheet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shift, but it's not the end of the world. At work I'd treat it as another tool people have to learn, and I'd say that nobody should sign off on its work blind. I'd keep an open mind with my friends but say to keep an eye on their own skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it hits my path directly. The operations team I interned with already ran about half its checks through software, and they hired no new juniors after me. If the entry level is what shrinks, I'm in the group that gets squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move from using AI now and then to using it every day, since that's what employers will expect. I'd take a course in data analysis and a short course on how to audit AI outputs. I'd try for jobs that are about checking and explaining, like internal audit or compliance, because they need someone to be accountable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mixed bag. A bit nervous, a bit determined. It feels like a puzzle I can work on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools now and then. What for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly to summarise long reports and to check my formulas. It's good for the first draft and weak when the facts matter, so I always check. Knowing when the tool is wrong is the skill I think employers will pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the payments company where you interned do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They kept the team at the same size and said no one would be replaced, and didn't hire. A quiet freeze, in other words. I'd expect more of the same, with the juniors the first to feel it.

I'd tell friends to keep an eye on their own **skills**.
think: The operations team I interned with already ran about **half** its checks through software.

Apply for internal audit and **compliance** roles that need someone accountable.
feel: **Nervous** and determined: it feels like a puzzle I can work on.

Steady style: moves once the **proof** is clear, then moves fully.

steps.text: Use an AI assistant every day for formulas and report summaries

Apply for internal audit and compliance roles
Do an evening data analysis course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that this is too fast and nobody can plan around it. I'd say it to anyone who asked, in a calm way, and I'd want to hear what the government plans. I wouldn't post anything online until I knew more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm frightened, and I'm not going to pretend I'm not. All of my training is for thinking work, and that's the first to go. The only comfort is that the robots arrive three years after, but I can't plan a whole life around that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make a list of every job that depends on a person being there, like care, hospitality, and trades, and apply to those. I'd talk to my parents about whether the taxi could be shared with a second driver. And I'd email my lender, explain the situation, and ask for a pause or a lower rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, with a little numbness. If I let myself think about it too long I stop being useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is not much time for a spreadsheet person. What would be on your list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd pay the minimum, live on the cheapest food, and sell what I can. I'd keep working and taking whatever hours come, because the loan doesn't go away. I'd hope for a policy change, since a lot of us would be in the same boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the lender didn't give you any relief?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thing I'd regret is the years I spent preparing for a job that vanished. But I'd rather have the degree than not, because it taught me how to think and learn.

say: This is too fast and nobody can **plan** around it.
I'd want to hear what the **government** plans before posting anything.
think: All my training is for thinking work, and that goes **first**.
Robots arriving three years later is a comfort, but I can't plan a **life** around it.
do: List jobs that need a person present, like **care**, hospitality and trades, and apply.
Ask my parents about a second **driver** for the taxi.
Email my lender to ask for a **pause** or lower rate.
feel: **Scared** with a little numbness: thinking too long stops me being useful.
S2.quote: The thing I'd regret is the years I spent preparing for a job that vanished.
fieldNote: Tries to stay **orderly** even when frightened, as her spreadsheet habit suggests.
Looks to **parents'** taxi and hands-on work but doesn't lean on them for money.
Admits her **fear** plainly rather than hiding it.

steps.text: List and apply to care, hospitality and trade jobs needing presence
Ask my parents about a second driver for the taxi
Email the lender for a payment pause or lower rate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good deal of time, and we should use it to get ready. I'd tell people to look at what jobs don't disappear in a hurry. I'd avoid scaring anyone, but I'd be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's manageable if I move fast now. If I could get a job within the next six months, I'd have about four years of real experience, and that would make me more valuable to a firm that needs people to check the machines. I'd also have time to pay a good chunk of the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first decent finance job, then learn everything I can about audit and compliance. I'd put 450 a month at the loan and keep a three-month cushion. In year three I'd review it, and if the field looked shaky I'd train for something that needs a person, like financial advice for families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More settled, because I can lay it out as steps. Steps are what keep me calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. How would you sequence it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First the job, then the money cushion, then the loan, then the retraining decision in year three. That order stops me from spending energy on the wrong thing at the wrong time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would convince you it's time to switch fields?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd switch if the firms around me stopped hiring juniors altogether, or if two or three people in my network lost their jobs. That would tell me the clock is real. Until then, I'd keep going.

say: Five years is a good deal of **time**, and we should use it.
Look at what jobs don't disappear in a **hurry**.
think: It's manageable if I move **fast** now.
A job in six months gives four years of **experience** and a chunk of the loan paid.

Put **450** a month at the loan and keep a three-month cushion.

feel: More **settled**, because I can lay it out as steps.
S3.quote: First the job, then the money cushion, then the loan, then the retraining decision in year three.

steps.text: Take the first decent finance job and learn audit work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decade, and that's long enough to plan. I'd bring it up with my friends as a topic, but not with any alarm. I'd be curious to hear what other people plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm fairly comfortable. If I get a job in the next year I'd have a full career's first stage, and I'd be able to move toward the parts that last. The debt is the main thing, and in ten years I'd have it gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a finance job, qualify as an accountant, and learn how to supervise AI. I'd save for a flat deposit and look at moving out of the shared house in three or four years. I'd also help my parents plan for the taxi's replacement, because even if driving goes, that's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with some leftover worry about the debt. I can see how it works out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. What changes in your life, beyond work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Beyond work, it changes where I live and when I can think about a family. If I'm secure by 27, I'd think about buying a small flat and having a family in my early thirties. A longer runway means I don't have to put things off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum and dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say you don't have to worry about me, and that they should look after my gran and themselves. I'd ask my dad to think about what comes after driving a taxi, and I'd help him do it.

say: A decade is long enough to **plan**, and I'd raise it with friends without alarm.
I'd be curious what other people **plan**.

The debt is the main thing, and in ten years it would be **gone**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two year one. I make plans, and plans need time. With a loan, a shared room and no savings, two years leaves no cushion and no way to reorganise. What would help is a loan pause, a public scheme that places graduates, and honest numbers from firms about hiring.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not as calm as I sound. I put everything in a spreadsheet so I don't panic. But I can see the numbers, and I know how few places there are.

headlineQuote: I'm not as calm as I sound. I put everything in a spreadsheet so I don't panic.
portrait: Uma is 23, top of her finance class, in a rented room in **Calderbrook** and owing 40,000.
Her parents are a taxi driver and a carer, with no spare money, so she carries the loan alone.
She tracks everything in a **spreadsheet**, moves once the evidence is clear, and widens her search steadily.
Her mood eases with time, from alarmed at two years to calm at ten, because plans need runway.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario, because she plans carefully and two years leaves no cushion.
whatWouldHelp: A **loan pause**, a public graduate placement scheme and honest hiring figures from firms.
